Triggers.value: Feeling physically restrained or held down

Memory.value: When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory
The memory feels like it belongs to someone else rather than to me
There are parts of the event that I simply cannot remember no matter how hard I try

vignette:
Amara, a 54-year-old judge, could not remember most of what happened during the three days she was held in that concrete cell. When she tried to deliberately recall the events—as she often did during sleepless nights or when a therapist gently pressed her—the memory refused to surface, leaving only a blank, buzzing space. The entire ordeal felt as though it had happened to someone else, a stranger whose life she had glimpsed in a documentary. There were gaps, whole stretches of time that simply did not exist in her mind: the moment she was taken from her car, the drive to the unknown location, the final release. What remained was not coherent narrative but sensory fragments—and those fragments had a life of their own.

In the courtroom, it was always the sounds that came first. A defendant, a middle-aged man charged with embezzlement, began to breathe heavily as the prosecutor outlined the evidence. The rhythm—shallow, rapid, with a slight rattle—cut through the gavel and the whispers. Amara’s own throat tightened. In that instant, the sensory fragment unlocked: she was back in the cell, and the guard was standing over her, his breath hot and uneven, the sound the only constant in the dark. The memory did not arrive as a full scene; it was more like a sudden, overwhelming conviction that the heavy breathing was here, in her present, pressing against her. She could smell it too: a cheap, cloying cologne that one of the interrogators had worn, the same scent that lingered in the courtroom whenever a particular attorney walked past. The memory, when it came through a trigger, was never complete—it was sharp and intrusive but also alien, as if she were watching a stranger being suffocated by her own senses.

Each time a trigger brought back a fragment of the memory—the sound, the smell, the feeling of her wrists being pinned—it made her more vigilant to those very cues. In the weeks following one upsetting hearing where a clerk’s heavy breathing had sent her reeling, Amara found herself scanning the room for anyone who breathed audibly, her attention snagging on every intake of air. The memory of being restrained, of her arms twisted behind her back, stayed with her long after the courtroom cleared. When she sat in her high-backed chair behind the bench, the pressure of the wood against her shoulders could feel like hands holding her down. That tactile sensation, in turn, triggered another flash—her wrists being cuffed, the metal digging in—and the loop tightened. She would become acutely aware of the cologne of the attorney approaching the bench, and the olfactory trigger would flood her with the same fragment: the interrogator leaning in, the smell overwhelming, her mind going blank.

What frightened her most was the gaps. She could not explain to herself why she was certain the heavy breathing meant she was in danger, because she could not retrieve the full narrative of what had happened next. The memory felt unreliable, like a stranger’s story, yet it governed her days. She had come to believe that if she could just remember—if she could close the gaps—the triggers would lose their power. But the more she tried to access the memory deliberately, the more it slipped away, and the more the triggers came unbidden.

Amara finally sought help after a morning when she nearly excused the jury for the day because the heat from the overhead lights felt like someone pressing her shoulders down. She told her colleague she felt unwell, and in the privacy of her chambers, she placed her hands flat on the desk to feel her own voluntary control. She was afraid that the next trigger would arrive when she could not compose herself—during a sentencing, perhaps—and that it would undo the authority she had worked two decades to build. What she hoped, in a quiet part of her mind, was for the memory to stop feeling like someone else’s—and for the courtroom to stop being a stage for fragments she could no longer command.
